I don't know that they're pursuing that, but it's because sometimes people can have different points of view. The view of in my role as your attorney is that the Civil Service Board has the authority to approve or deny the recommendations coming from the police department for these lists. Ultimately, civil service boards were created for the purpose of having that that extra layer of sort of objectivity so that there wasn't cronyism. And this was from way back when, when these boards were created. And because of that, you do have the authority to determine whether or not you've received adequate information on a particular recommendation. So here you have the recommendation for disqualification on three people. Now, balanced against that is the fact that sometimes the recommendation is based on something that if put in the public arena, could be potentially embarrassing or harmful to a person's rights to privacy. I don't know what some examples of that would be, but it could be something that just doesn't really need to be played out in the public to that degree. You have the ability as a board to decide, well, we didn't get adequate information for disqualification, therefore we're not going to disqualify. Or you can decide that you want to hear more about it in an executive session so that you can consider the details without exposing them to public consideration. You can ask for more information. You can say, bring it back in a month, but we want more. The real question is up to the board. Like I said, one option is if you truly don't feel like you have sufficient information, one option is to say this is not sufficient to disqualify an applicant and therefore we're not going to disqualify. But you also may find ways to ask for more information. If you were to directly just say, I want to hear the information here now in this meeting, one of the potential risks, and it's not always a hardcore legal risk, it's more a question of what kind of decorum you want in your meetings, you could end up having your officers who are aware of the disqualifying information putting it right out there on YouTube for anyone to see, and sometimes that's potentially embarrassing beyond what is necessary to your process.
